title: Seven days
hookLine: Maya dies a week after the birth; her sister Mahapajapati raises him as her own

cards: Queen Maya dies. Until now the story has been all wonders: a shining elephant in a dream, a branch bending to a queen's hand, gods cheering in the sky, a sage weeping over a cradle.
It read like a fairy tale, and fairy tales don't usually turn this hard. The baby everyone says will change the world is one week old, and he has no mother.

teach.b: A discourse says it plainly, as if it were simply part of the pattern: seven days after a future buddha is born, his mother dies. No long scene. It adds one line: she reappears in a heaven, the Tusita heaven.
A later story tells of the Buddha, years afterward, going to teach her among the gods.
But on earth a newborn has lost his mother, and here's who steps in: Maya's younger sister, Mahapajapati Gotami. She's also married to King Suddhodana, and she has a baby son of her own, Nanda.
The commentaries say she gives her own son to nurses and nurses Siddhattha herself, raising him as her own. Years later it's remembered out loud.
In one discourse, Mahapajapati brings the Buddha a gift of new cloth, and his attendant Ananda speaks up for her.
She was his mother's sister, Ananda says, his nurse, his foster mother; she nursed him when his own mother died. A debt of care, said in front of everyone.
Her own story doesn't end there; she'll come back later on this path, with a story of her own.
Today is about a child whose first great loss came before he could remember it, and a woman who chose to love him as if he were hers.
The tradition keeps them both: the mother who carried him, and the mother who raised him.

how: Buddhists honor both Maya, the Buddha's mother, and Mahapajapati Gotami, who raised him; Mahapajapati is remembered as the first Buddhist nun, and Buddhist teaching stresses gratitude to parents and those who raise us.

games.q: you're Mahapajapati. your sister has died, leaving a newborn. you have a baby of your own. what do you do, in the texts?
o: give your own son to nurses, and nurse your nephew yourself.
send the baby to his mother's family.

practice: Think of someone who did some of your raising, whether or not they had to: a parent, a grandparent, a stepparent, an aunt, a coach, a teacher, a neighbor who fed you. Picture their face and thank them silently.
If that relationship is complicated, thank the part that helped and leave the rest.
